prerequisites.title: Algebra Essentials (catch-up)
prerequisites.summary: Real numbers, variables, simplifying expressions, solving linear equations. From OpenStax Ch 1.1.

objectives: Classify real numbers as natural, whole, integer, rational, or irrational.

explanation.intro: Precalculus assumes fluency with the algebra you met in high school. This topic compresses the essentials from OpenStax §1.1 so you have a solid launch pad.

sections.heading: Real numbers
sections.body: The real numbers are all the numbers on a number line. They split into rational numbers (ratios of integers, like 3/4 and -2) and irrational numbers (like √2 and π).
bullets: Natural: 1, 2, 3, …
Rational: a/b with integer a, b ≠ 0
Irrational: cannot be written as a/b

sections.heading: Order of operations
sections.body: Evaluate in this order: parentheses, exponents, multiplication/division (left to right), addition/subtraction (left to right). PEMDAS.
bullets: Tip: 'PEMDAS' is a checklist, not a license to ignore left-to-right.
Tip: a − b − c = a − b − c; a/b/c = a/(b·c).

sections.heading: Linear equations
sections.body: A linear equation in x is of the form ax + b = c with a ≠ 0. Solve by isolating x: subtract b from both sides, then divide by a.
bullets: Always distribute before collecting like terms.
Check by substituting the solution back in.

prerequisites.title: Exponents & Scientific Notation
prerequisites.summary: Exponent rules, integer and rational exponents, scientific notation. From OpenStax §1.2.

objectives: Apply the product, quotient, and power rules for exponents.

explanation.intro: Exponent rules are the silent engine behind nearly every precalculus formula. OpenStax §1.2 walks through them in order of difficulty.

sections.heading: Product & quotient rules
sections.body: When multiplying powers with the same base, add exponents: aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. When dividing, subtract: aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ.
bullets: These only work when the bases are the same.
Examples: 2³·2⁴ = 2⁷ = 128, 5⁶/5² = 5⁴ = 625.

sections.heading: Power rules
sections.body: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ. (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ.
bullets: Distribute a power to every factor inside.
(2x³)⁴ = 2⁴x¹² = 16x¹².

sections.heading: Zero & negative exponents
sections.body: a⁰ = 1 (for a ≠ 0). a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. Negative exponents flip the factor to the reciprocal.
bullets: Tip: rewrite 1/x⁻³ as x³, not 1/x³.

sections.heading: Scientific notation
sections.body: A number in scientific notation has the form a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ |a| < 10. The exponent n is the number of places the decimal moved.

explanation.intro: Polynomials are the building blocks of nearly every function you'll meet. From OpenStax §§1.4–1.5.

sections.heading: Multiplying polynomials
sections.body: Distribute every term of one factor across every term of the other. For (a + b)(c + d) you get ac + ad + bc + bd — FOIL when both factors are binomials.

sections.body: Try these in order: GCF, then difference of squares, then trinomial, then grouping.

Trinomial x² + bx + c: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.

explanation.intro: Precalculus happens on the coordinate plane. From OpenStax §§2.1–2.2.

sections.heading: Cartesian plane
sections.body: Each point is an ordered pair (x, y). x tells you horizontal position (right is positive), y tells you vertical position (up is positive).
bullets: The axes split the plane into four quadrants.

sections.heading: Slope
sections.body: Slope = rise/run = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). It's the rate at which y changes as x increases by 1.
bullets: Positive slope: line goes up to the right.
Negative slope: line goes down to the right.
Zero slope: horizontal line.
Undefined slope: vertical line.

sections.heading: Forms of a line
sections.body: Slope-intercept: y = mx + b (m = slope, b = y-intercept). Point-slope: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). Standard: Ax + By = C.
bullets: Use point-slope when you know one point and the slope.
Convert to slope-intercept to read m and b easily.

sections.body: Set the denominator to zero (after simplifying). Each root gives a vertical asymptote or a hole.

sections.heading: Horizontal asymptotes
sections.body: Compare degrees: if deg(num) < deg(den), y = 0. If equal, ratio of leading coefficients. If greater, no horizontal asymptote (maybe a slant one).

sections.heading: Holes
sections.body: Common factors in numerator and denominator create holes (removable discontinuities), not asymptotes.

stepByStep.title: Find the oblique asymptote of f(x) = (x² + x) / (x − 1).

steps.label: Polynomial long division
steps.math: x² ÷ x = x. Multiply: x(x−1) = x²−x. Subtract: (x²+x)−(x²−x) = 2x.

steps.label: Final answer
steps.math: Oblique asymptote: y = x + 2 (from the quotient).

steps.label: Behavior

steps.label: Final answer
steps.math: Hyperbola in QI and QII. VA: x = 0. HA: y = 0. Even (symmetric about y-axis).

steps.label: Horizontal asymptotes

steps.explanation: 1/x² never crosses the x-axis and is never negative.

steps.label: Symmetry
steps.math: y = 1/x: odd (origin symmetric). y = 1/x²: even (y-axis symmetric).

steps.label: Final answer
steps.math: y = 1/x oscillates between positive and negative. y = 1/x² is always positive, decays faster, symmetric about y-axis.

topics.summary: Horizontal-line test, finding the inverse, domain/range swap. From Lippman & Rasmussen §1.6 and OpenStax §3.7.

objectives: Determine whether a function is one-to-one.

explanation.intro: An inverse function undoes what the original does. Only one-to-one functions can have inverses.

sections.heading: One-to-one
sections.body: Every output comes from exactly one input. Horizontal-line test for graphs.

sections.heading: Finding the inverse
sections.body: Replace f(x) with y. Swap x and y. Solve for y. The result is f⁻¹(x).

sections.heading: Domain & range swap
sections.body: Domain of f = range of f⁻¹. Range of f = domain of f⁻¹.

steps.label: Horizontal-line test
steps.math: y = 1/x passes the HLT — each horizontal line crosses at most once (except y = 0).

steps.label: Final answer
steps.math: f is one-to-one on each interval (−∞, 0) and (0, ∞). f⁻¹(x) = 1/x (self-inverse).
steps.explanation: f(f(x)) = x for all x ≠ 0. It's its own inverse.

stepByStep.title: Restrict the domain of y = √x so that an inverse exists. What is the inverse?
stepByStep.prompt: Note the domain restriction and swap.

steps.label: Original function
steps.explanation: Square root is the principal (non-negative) root.

steps.label: Restriction
steps.math: Standard restriction: x ≥ 0. This makes it strictly increasing.

steps.label: Find inverse
steps.math: x = √y → x² = y. So f⁻¹(x) = x².
steps.explanation: Swap x and y, then solve for y.

steps.label: Final answer
steps.explanation: Domain of f⁻¹ = [0, ∞), which matches the range of f.

stepByStep.title: If f(g(x)) = x and g(f(x)) = x for all x in the domain, what can you conclude?

steps.label: f(g(x)) = x
steps.math: f and g are inverses: g undoes f. g(x) is in the domain of f.
steps.explanation: f∘g = identity on domain of g.

steps.label: g(f(x)) = x
steps.math: g and f are inverses: f undoes g. f(x) is in the domain of g.
steps.explanation: g∘f = identity on domain of f.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.math: f and g are inverses of each other.
steps.explanation: Both compositions equal x — this is the two-way inverse condition.

steps.label: Final answer
steps.math: f and g are inverse functions (f⁻¹ = g and g⁻¹ = f).
steps.explanation: Both conditions must hold for a true inverse relationship.

explanation.intro: An exponential function has the form f(x) = a·bˣ with b > 0 and b ≠ 1.

sections.heading: Form

sections.body: log_b x = ln x / ln b = log x / log b.

explanation.intro: The six trig functions each have a characteristic graph. They share many parameters you can read off the formula.

sections.heading: y = A sin(Bx − C) + D
sections.body: Amplitude = |A|. Period = 2π/|B|. Phase shift = C/B. Vertical shift = D.

sections.heading: Reciprocal functions
sections.body: csc, sec, cot are reciprocals of sin, cos, tan. Their graphs have vertical asymptotes wherever the original is zero.

sections.heading: Tangent
sections.body: y = tan x has period π and vertical asymptotes at x = π/2 + kπ.

steps.label: Period

topics.title: Fundamental Trig Identities
topics.summary: Reciprocal, quotient, Pythagorean, and cofunction identities. From Lippman & Rasmussen §7.1 and Yoshiwara §5.2.

objectives: State and apply the reciprocal, quotient, and Pythagorean identities.
Use cofunction identities to rewrite trig functions of complementary angles.

explanation.intro: Identities are equations that hold for every angle in the domain. They are the algebra of trigonometry.

sections.heading: Reciprocal
sections.body: csc θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ.

sections.heading: Quotient
sections.body: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, cot θ = cos θ / sin θ.

sections.heading: Pythagorean
sections.body: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ. 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.

sections.heading: Cofunction
sections.body: sin(π/2 − θ) = cos θ. cos(π/2 − θ) = sin θ. tan(π/2 − θ) = cot θ.

examples.title: If sin θ = 3/5 and θ is in Q I, find cos θ.
steps: sin² + cos² = 1 → cos² = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25 → cos = 4/5 (positive in Q I).

stepByStep.title: Simplify (1 − sin² θ) / sin θ.

steps.label: Separate
steps.math: cos θ · (cos θ / sin θ) = cos θ · cot θ

stepByStep.title: Verify:  sin² θ + cos² θ = 1.
stepByStep.prompt: Recall this is the Pythagorean identity.

steps.label: From the unit circle
steps.math: x² + y² = 1. On the unit circle, x = cos θ, y = sin θ.
steps.explanation: This identity is derived from the unit circle equation.

steps.label: Algebraic verification
steps.math: sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 for all θ.
steps.explanation: No further algebra needed — this is the definition of the Pythagorean identity.

steps.label: Rearrangements
steps.math: sin² θ = 1 − cos² θ. cos² θ = 1 − sin² θ.
steps.explanation: These are used to convert between sin and cos.

steps.label: Final answer
steps.math: sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 is the fundamental Pythagorean identity for all real θ.
steps.explanation: All other trig identities derive from it.

stepByStep.title: Simplify  sec θ · sin θ · cot θ.
stepByStep.prompt: Rewrite everything in terms of sin and cos.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.math: sec θ · sin θ · cot θ = (1/cos θ) · sin θ · (cos θ / sin θ)

steps.label: Cancel
steps.math: = (1/cos θ) · sin θ · (cos θ / sin θ) = (1 · sin θ · cos θ) / (cos θ · sin θ)
steps.explanation: cos θ cancels; sin θ cancels.

stepByStep.title: Simplify  (sin x + cos x)².

steps.label: Expand
steps.math: (sin x + cos x)² = sin² x + 2 sin x cos x + cos² x

steps.label: Result
steps.explanation: Also note: 2 sin x cos x = sin(2x).

stepByStep.title: Express tan θ in terms of sin θ only.

steps.label: Recall tan θ
steps.math: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
steps.explanation: We need to express cos θ in terms of sin θ.

steps.label: From identity
steps.math: sin² θ + cos² θ = 1 → cos² θ = 1 − sin² θ → cos θ = ±√(1 − sin² θ)
steps.explanation: Take the appropriate sign based on the quadrant.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.math: tan θ = sin θ / (±√(1 − sin² θ))
steps.explanation: The sign of cos θ depends on the quadrant.

steps.label: Final answer
steps.math: tan θ = sin θ / √(1 − sin² θ) in QI; tan θ = −sin θ / √(1 − sin² θ) in QII.
steps.explanation: Must specify the sign of cos θ from the quadrant.

topics.summary: Formulas for sin(A ± B), cos(A ± B), tan(A ± B); double and half-angle identities. From Yoshiwara §8.0 and OpenStax §9.3.

objectives: Apply the sum and difference identities for sine, cosine, and tangent.

explanation.intro: Angle-addition identities let you compute trig values that aren't on the unit circle by combining ones that are.

sections.heading: Sum formulas
sections.body: sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B. cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B.

sections.heading: Difference formulas
sections.body: Replace + with −; sign of the B-terms flips. tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B) / (1 ∓ tan A tan B).

sections.heading: Double-angle
sections.body: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ. cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ = 2 cos²θ − 1.

sections.heading: Half-angle
sections.body: sin(θ/2) = ±√((1 − cos θ)/2). cos(θ/2) = ±√((1 + cos θ)/2). Sign picked by the quadrant of θ/2.

topics.title: Conic Sections: Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, Hyperbolas
topics.summary: Identify and graph the four conic sections by their algebraic form. Master the standard equations, foci, vertices, and eccentricity. From OpenStax §§12.1–12.4.

objectives: Classify a conic by its algebraic form.

explanation.intro: A conic section is the curve formed by intersecting a plane with a double cone. Four types: circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola.

sections.heading: Circles
sections.body: A circle is the set of points equidistant from a center. Standard: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².

sections.heading: Ellipses
sections.body: An ellipse is the set of points where the sum of distances to two foci is constant. Standard: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. Eccentricity 0 < e < 1.

sections.heading: Parabolas
sections.body: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus and a directrix. Standard: y = ax². Eccentricity e = 1.

sections.heading: Hyperbolas
sections.body: A hyperbola is the set of points where the absolute difference of distances to two foci is constant. Standard: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. Eccentricity e > 1.

sections.heading: Eccentricity
sections.body: Eccentricity e is the unifying measure. e = 0: circle. 0 < e < 1: ellipse. e = 1: parabola. e > 1: hyperbola.

topics.summary: Arithmetic and geometric sequences, partial sums, and an introduction to the Fibonacci sequence. From OpenStax §§13.1–13.3.

objectives: Identify arithmetic vs. geometric sequences.

explanation.intro: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers; a series is their sum. Two fundamental families: arithmetic (constant difference) and geometric (constant ratio).

sections.heading: Arithmetic sequences
sections.body: a_n = a₁ + (n−1)d, where d is the common difference.

sections.heading: Geometric sequences
sections.body: a_n = a₁ · r^(n−1), where r is the common ratio.

sections.heading: Geometric series
sections.body: S_n = a₁ · (1 − r^n)/(1 − r). For |r| < 1, infinite sum S = a₁/(1 − r).

sections.heading: Special sequences
sections.body: Fibonacci: each term is the sum of the two previous. Arithmetic and geometric are the main families you will see.
